title: Threat Group-3390
summary: Threat Group-3390 is a long-running intrusion set that public reporting, including work published by several vendors and by MITRE ATT&CK, associates with activity widely assessed by third parties as linked to a Chinese state-interest nexus, though no government has formally indicted or sanctioned the activity under this name, so the sponsorship claim rests on vendor analysis rather than official attribution. The cluster is tracked under many overlapping names, including Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse, Bronze Union, Earth Smilodon, and APT27, and different publishers have drawn the boundaries of those labels differently over time, with some activity reassigned between clusters as new evidence emerged. Reporting describes targeting of government ministries and agencies, defence and aerospace organisations, energy and critical infrastructure operators, gaming and technology companies, and organisations in the Middle East, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Europe, with additional victims reported in North America. The group is notable in open reporting for combining web-facing exploitation with heavy use of publicly available remote access tooling, which lowers the cost of operations and blurs the line between targeted intrusion and commodity compromise. Described tradecraft includes exploitation of public-facing applications for initial access, abuse of external remote services including web shells and remote management interfaces, credential dumping and reuse of valid administrator accounts, lateral movement over standard administrative protocols, scheduled task and service-based persistence, and exfiltration staged to attacker-controlled or legitimate third-party web services. Several reporting streams describe usage of custom downloaders alongside commodity tooling and an interest in harvesting intellectual property and email. Defenders should note that the group's reliance on administration-facing protocols means detection strategies centred on endpoint malware alone will miss significant portions of the intrusion lifecycle, and that the use of legitimate remote services makes allow-listing decisions consequential.
objectives: Explain how web shell persistence on an internet-facing server is detected and how to prioritise containment once found.
Detect abuse of external remote services and administrative protocols that blend with legitimate management traffic.
Analyse the risk of credential dumping and administrative account reuse when designing tiered administration controls.
Build detection logic for scheduled task and service creation used for persistence and evaluate its false positive profile.
Explain how staged exfiltration to legitimate third-party web services evades protocol-based egress controls and what replaces those controls.
Describe how cluster boundaries shift as vendors reassign activity and why that matters for indicator sharing.
Prioritise detection effort across web-facing exploitation, identity abuse, and lateral movement for an organisation in a targeted sector.

beginner.definition: Threat Group-3390 is a tracking name for a long-running spying group that security companies link to state interests in China. It is also called Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse and APT27. No government has formally named it, so the country link rests on company analysis. Different companies draw its edges differently.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group breaks into servers that face the internet, then leaves a small web page that works like a remote control. It also uses free, widely available administration tools. That mix makes its activity look like normal technical support work. If you only look for known malware, you will miss it. Watch your servers and your administrator accounts.
howItWorks: The group finds a weakness in a public website or server and exploits it.
They upload a web shell, a small script that runs commands through the website.
With that access they steal administrator passwords that are stored on the machine.
Those passwords let them log in to other computers using normal administrator tools.
They add scheduled tasks or services so their access survives a restart.
Stolen files are uploaded to ordinary web services, which rarely look suspicious.
beginner.example: Picture a shop with a public front door and a small back room. Someone slips a note under the door that says, trade this note for any item you like. Staff read the note and hand goods through the wall, because it looks like a normal order. Nobody broke a lock. The shop was simply never designed to notice a strange instruction.
takeaways: Keep internet-facing servers patched, and watch for files added to web folders.
Treat administrator tools used at odd hours as a possible intrusion.
Stolen data often leaves through ordinary websites, so watch uploads as well.
